title: THE BIBLE ACTUALLY EXPLAINS WHY GOD DIDN’T TAKE ISRAEL THE SHORT WAY
paragraphs: THE BIBLE ACTUALLY EXPLAINS WHY GOD DIDN’T TAKE ISRAEL THE SHORT WAY
The road was shorter. God knew it. Israel could have taken it. But God deliberately led them another way—and the reason may completely change how you interpret the road you are walking right now.
There was a shorter road.
That is what makes this story hurt.
Because sometimes the hardest thing about following God is not that you cannot see another way.
You can.
You can see the shorter way.
The quicker answer.
The easier route.
The prayer that could have been answered by now.
The door God could have opened.
The relationship He could have restored.
The opportunity He could have allowed.
The breakthrough that seems as though it should have happened months—or years—ago.
And somewhere between what God promised and where you are standing, a question begins whispering inside you:
“Lord… why are we going this way?”
Israel could have asked exactly that question.
They had just escaped Egypt.

After generations of bondage, the impossible had happened. Pharaoh had finally released them. The blood of the Passover lamb had marked Israel’s houses. Judgment had passed over them. Their chains were behind them.
Freedom was finally in front of them.
And then Scripture tells us something astonishing.
There was a shorter road.
God did not take it.
Exodus 13:17 records:
“וְלֹא־נָחָם אֱלֹהִים דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים כִּי קָרוֹב הוּא”
Ve-lo nacham Elohim derekh eretz Pelishtim, ki qarov hu.
In context:
God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near.
Read those final Hebrew words again:
כִּי קָרוֹב הוּא — ki qarov hu.
It was near.
God was not lost.
God had not miscalculated the route.
God did not need directions.
The wilderness was not an accidental detour caused by divine incompetence.
The text explicitly tells us that God knew there was a nearer route—and chose not to lead Israel through it.
Then Scripture tells us why.
And this is where the passage becomes painfully personal.
God said:
“פֶּן־יִנָּחֵם הָעָם בִּרְאֹתָם מִלְחָמָה וְשָׁבוּ מִצְרָיְמָה”
Pen-yinnachem ha'am bir'otam milchamah, ve-shavu Mitzraymah.
In other words, God knew that when the people saw war, they might change their minds…
and return to Egypt.
Not because Egypt was good.
Not because Pharaoh loved them.
Not because slavery was better than freedom.
But because human beings can become so accustomed to bondage that familiar suffering begins to feel safer than unfamiliar dependence on God.
That is frightening.
You can be delivered from Egypt and still carry an Egypt-shaped reflex inside you.
You can walk out physically while part of your heart still knows how to run back.
Israel had witnessed miracles that should have made doubt impossible.
They had seen water become blood.
They had watched Egypt shaken by plague after plague.
They had watched God distinguish between His people and their oppressors.
They had eaten the Passover under the protection of sacrificial blood.
They had watched the most powerful ruler around finally surrender to the command of God.
And yet God knew something about them that perhaps they did not yet know about themselves.
They were free…
but fragile.
Delivered…
but not yet mature.
Out of Egypt…
but still capable of returning to Egypt when fear became louder than faith.
So God did something that probably made no sense from ground level.
He led them around.
Exodus 13:18 says:
“וַיַּסֵּב אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָעָם דֶּרֶךְ הַמִּדְבָּר”
Vayyassev Elohim et-ha'am derekh hammidbar.
God led the people around by the way of the wilderness.
Around.
Not straight through.
Around.
There are seasons when that word feels like your entire life.
You thought you would be further along by now.
You thought the marriage would have healed by now.
You thought the grief would hurt less by now.
You thought your children would have returned to God by now.
You thought the ministry would have grown by now.
You thought the financial pressure would have broken by now.
You thought after everything you survived, surely the road ahead would finally become simple.
Instead…
around.
Another wilderness.
Another unanswered prayer.
Another closed door.
Another season watching other people arrive somewhere you have been begging God to take you.
And when you cannot understand the route, you can easily begin questioning the Guide.
But Exodus 13 gives us a window into something Israel could not see.
God knew what was waiting on the shorter road.
And God knew what was still vulnerable inside the people walking it.
That distinction matters.

We should not casually tell every suffering person, “God caused this because you weren't ready.” Scripture does not give us permission to explain every delay, tragedy, illness, rejection, or loss with one formula.
But Exodus 13 does reveal something true about God's character:
God can know dangers His people cannot see, and His guidance is not limited to what appears efficient to us.
The shortest route is not automatically the wisest route.
The fastest answer is not automatically the most merciful answer.
And what feels like unnecessary distance from where you stand may look very different from the perspective of the God who sees the whole road.
Israel saw mileage.
God saw warfare.
Israel saw inconvenience.
God saw the possibility of retreat.
Israel could measure the distance between Egypt and Canaan.
Only God could fully measure what fear might do inside their hearts.
And maybe that exposes something in us.
Because we love a God who delivers quickly.
We struggle with a God who leads slowly.
We celebrate the Red Sea opening.
We rarely celebrate the road that takes us to it.
We shout about promises.
We whisper complaints about process.

We want God to remove Pharaoh, open the door, defeat the enemy, heal the wound, restore the relationship, fix the finances, answer the prayer—and then take us by the fastest possible road into everything He has promised.
But Scripture refuses to reduce God to a divine shortcut machine.
He is Lord.
He leads.
And sometimes His leadership will contradict your preferred route without contradicting His goodness.
There is something else here we cannot miss.
The Israelites left Egypt equipped for battle.
Exodus 13:18 describes them with the Hebrew word:
וַחֲמֻשִׁים — vachamushim.
The term has been understood in the sense of being equipped or arrayed for battle.
Think about the tension.
They looked ready for battle.
Yet God knew what seeing battle could do to them.
That will preach to the places we hide.
Because appearing equipped and being inwardly prepared are not always the same thing.
You can carry a Bible and still be terrified.
You can serve in church and still have wounds nobody knows about.
You can post Scriptures while crying after everyone goes to sleep.
You can know worship songs and still struggle to trust God when the lights go out.
You can tell everybody, “God is good,” while privately wondering why He has allowed your road to become so long.
You can look armed for battle…
and God can still know exactly where you are vulnerable.
And remarkably, He does not abandon Israel because of that vulnerability.
He leads them.
That is grace.
God knew they might turn back, yet He did not send them back.
He changed the route.
Somebody reading this needs that sentence.
God knew how frightened they could become and continued leading them anyway.
Their weakness did not surprise Him.
Their immaturity did not cancel His covenant.
Their capacity to panic did not erase His faithfulness.
The wilderness would expose terrible things in Israel. They would complain. They would doubt. They would romanticize Egypt. They would rebel.
Scripture does not sanitize them.
And Scripture does not sanitize us either.
Because if we are painfully honest, some of us have wanted Egypt again too.
Not literal Egypt.
Your Egypt had another name.
The addiction Jesus pulled you away from.
The relationship you knew was destroying you.
The secret messages you promised you would stop sending.
The bitterness you keep reopening.
The pornography you deleted and then searched for again.
The approval addiction that keeps controlling your decisions.
The old crowd.
The old habits.
The old compromises.
The old version of yourself that Jesus called you to leave behind.
You know it was bondage.
Yet when following Christ became costly, part of you started remembering bondage selectively.
That is what fear does.
It edits your memories.
It makes slavery look stable.
It makes compromise look comfortable.
It makes yesterday's chains look easier than today's wilderness.
Israel would eventually say things that revealed how deeply Egypt still lived in their imagination.
And before we judge them, we should examine ourselves.
How many times have we prayed for freedom and then missed the very thing God freed us from?
How many times have we asked Jesus to rescue us, only to become uncomfortable when rescue required transformation?
We want Christ to save us from consequences while leaving our idols untouched.
But Jesus did not die merely to make your Egypt more comfortable.
He came to set captives free.
And this is where Exodus begins pointing beyond itself toward the greater redemption story fulfilled in Christ.
Passover stands at the doorway of Israel's exodus.
Blood marked the houses.
Judgment passed over.
A people in bondage were brought out.
And the New Testament deliberately uses Passover language for Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 5:7:
The Exodus was real history, but it also participates in the great biblical pattern of redemption that reaches its fulfillment in Jesus.
Our deepest Pharaoh is not a human king.
Our deepest bondage is sin.
Our deepest problem is not merely that life has become difficult.
It is that humanity is alienated from a holy God by sin and cannot rescue itself.
And Jesus did what no self-improvement plan could accomplish.
He came for sinners.
He lived without sin.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Jesus does not merely show prisoners how to decorate their cells.
He breaks chains.
He forgives sinners.
He reconciles rebels to God.
He gives new life.
But following Jesus does not mean every road afterward becomes short.
That false promise has wounded too many believers.
Sometimes following Jesus leads through wilderness.
Sometimes obedience costs you friendships.
Sometimes repentance means deleting numbers you secretly wanted to keep.
Sometimes healing involves finally admitting what happened.
Sometimes forgiveness takes you into painful places where Christ teaches your heart to release vengeance without pretending evil was acceptable.
Sometimes sanctification feels slower than you expected.
Sometimes you pray and heaven appears silent.
Sometimes you obey God and circumstances initially become harder.
Israel obeyed God into a route that looked less efficient.
Soon they would stand between Pharaoh's army and the sea.
Imagine being there.
The wilderness behind you.
Water in front of you.
An army approaching.
And perhaps someone whispers:
“We should have taken the other road.”
Then the sea opens.
Suddenly the road that looked wrong becomes the stage on which God's glory is displayed.

But notice carefully: Exodus 13 does not say God took the longer road merely so Israel could have a dramatic testimony. The explicit reason given is His knowledge that encountering war on the nearer route could cause them to turn back.
That makes the story even more beautiful.
God's sovereignty is not an excuse for us to invent explanations Scripture never gives.
It is an invitation to trust the God who sees what we cannot.
Maybe you do not know why your road has been long.
I will not insult your pain by pretending I know.
Maybe nobody on Facebook knows.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe your family does not understand.
Maybe you have prayed until you ran out of impressive words and finally reduced your prayer to:
“Jesus… please.”
There are questions faith does not answer by pretending they do not hurt.
Faith brings those questions to God.
The cross gives us the strongest reason Christians have for trusting His heart when we cannot trace His hand.
At Calvary, the disciples saw catastrophe.
The Messiah was crucified.
Hope appeared buried.
The One they believed would redeem Israel was hanging between criminals.
If anyone had judged God's plan by Friday afternoon alone, everything would have looked horribly wrong.
But Friday was not the end of the story.
Sunday came.
The stone moved.
Christ rose.
Death lost its final claim.
Sin's debt had been answered.
And the greatest apparent defeat became the center of God's redemptive victory.
That does not mean every earthly tragedy receives a neat explanation before heaven.
It means the Christian's confidence rests ultimately not in understanding every road but in Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
So perhaps the question is changing.
Instead of only asking:
“God, why haven't You taken me there yet?”
Perhaps another prayer needs to rise:
“Jesus, keep me faithful while You lead me.”
Because getting somewhere quickly is not the greatest goal of the Christian life.
Knowing Christ is.
Becoming like Christ is.
Remaining faithful to Christ is.
Arriving at eternity with Christ is.
The Promised Land was never proof that Israel had become impressive.
Their story was a story of grace.
Again and again, they failed.
Again and again, God remained faithful to His covenant purposes.
And that is why the Gospel Warrior message will always return here:
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him into an apostle of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Grace met him on a cross.
And you?
Maybe your story contains chapters you wish could be ripped from the book.
Maybe you have failed publicly.
Maybe you have sinned privately.
Maybe people know the version of you that you desperately wish they would forget.
Maybe you have walked with Jesus for years and still discovered places inside yourself that need repentance.
Do not run back to Egypt because you are ashamed of struggling in the wilderness.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Confess.
Come into the light.
The answer to your sin is not pretending you never sinned.
The answer is Jesus.
There is forgiveness at His cross.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a new identity that neither Pharaoh nor your past gets to name.
Your scandal does not outrank His grace.
Your failure does not possess greater authority than His cross.
Your darkest chapter does not get to write the final sentence if your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe now you understand why this story is so unforgettable.
God did not take Israel the short way because He knew something they did not.
He knew the road.
He knew the enemy.
He knew His people.
He knew their fear.
And still…
He led them.
So if you are in a wilderness right now, do not automatically assume you have been abandoned.
Examine yourself honestly. Search Scripture. Seek wise counsel. Repent wherever repentance is necessary.
But do not confuse a longer road with the absence of God.
In Exodus, the people on the longer road had something extraordinary.
A cloud by day.
Fire by night.
The presence of God went before them.
The wilderness was difficult.
But they were not alone.
And Christian, neither are you.
Jesus never promised His disciples an easy road. He promised something better than ease:
Himself.
If this exposed something hidden in you—especially a place where you have been tempted to return to an old bondage because following Jesus became difficult—be honest.
Somebody reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that another believer has cried, struggled, doubted, prayed—and discovered that Jesus was still faithful.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
Send it to the believer who nearly went back to Egypt.
Send it to the person who has stopped attending church.
Send it to the person who does not yet know Christ.
The road being longer does not mean God has lost the way.
Pray.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A ministry is not the Savior.
Jesus Christ is.

And if anything we create does not ultimately lead people toward Him, His Word, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, obedience, and transformation, then we have missed the reason for creating it.
So tonight, if you find yourself staring at the road you wish God had chosen…
remember Israel.
Remember the nearer road.
Remember the wilderness.
Remember the cloud.
Remember the fire.
Remember the sea.
Remember the blood of Passover.
And above everything else…
remember the cross and the empty tomb.
You may not understand why the road has been this long.
You may not know what tomorrow contains.
You may not be able to explain why God permitted one door to close while another remained painfully distant.
But if you belong to Jesus, your hope is not that every road will become short.
Your hope is that the One who gave Himself for you will never cease being faithful.
Keep walking.
Not because the wilderness is easy.
Not because you understand the map.
But because Christ is worthy.
And when your heart starts whispering that Egypt would have been easier, remember this:
Never trade the freedom Christ purchased for you just because the road of following Him became longer than you expected.
